notes.PA: No in-person early voting, so this is mail ballots returned. Pennsylvania's mail electorate is heavily Democratic whatever the year (about D+53 at 12 days out in 2022, when Republicans won the national House vote by 3), so it says little about direction; the slope fitted for mail-only states is small for that reason. Requests by party are shown for context.
notes.FL: Mail plus in-person. In-person early voting opens Oct 19 (Oct 24 in 2022, Oct 21 in 2024); until then this is mail only, and Florida Republicans moved toward mail after 2022. Florida's final early vote was R+6 in 2022 (result R+19) and R+9 in 2024 (result R+13).
notes.NV: Mail plus in-person, from the Secretary of State's daily files (UF Election Lab compiles them; Jon Ralston's blog reported the 2022 and 2024 leads used here). In-person opens Oct 17. 2022's early vote finished about D+1.5 and the Senate race was D+0.8; 2024's finished R+3.8 and the presidential race was R+3.1.
notes.CO: All-mail state; nearly every ballot is returned by mail or drop box. The Secretary of State posts a release each weekday from about three weeks out with returns by party; 2022 and 2024 points come from those spreadsheets.
notes.IA: Absentee ballots received, which in Iowa include ballots cast in person at the auditor's office. Iowa Democrats vote absentee far more than Republicans in every year (2022's absentee pool was D+19 while the Senate race was R+12), so the small mail-state slope applies. 2022 and 2024 points are the Secretary of State's daily reports as compiled by Bleeding Heartland.
notes.AZ: Early ballots returned, compiled from county reports by Stealth Analytics for UF Election Lab (Arizona has no official statewide daily file). No same-point baseline yet; the 2022 and 2024 final early votes are shown for context.

story.headline: The official same-point comparison with 2022 now rests on three states and still sits far below the polls: Florida (D+4.3 by registration after two days of in-person voting, vs. about D+2.7 at 14 days out in 2022), Colorado (D+9.0 vs. D+3.6) and Iowa pool to an implied national vote of about D+0.2 (±1.5), while Pennsylvania's first match with 2024 (D+43.9 vs. D+33.1, mail only) implies about D+2.4; the polls say D+8.1. Nevada's official Oct 20 reading is an even split, but that file's party counts cover only part of the mail ballots, while Jon Ralston's count had Democrats ahead by about 3.7 points. The news comparisons lean more Democratic: North Carolina's early vote is 38% ahead of 2022 with Republican in-person ballots down, Georgia's in-person count is 12% ahead and Texas opened 20% ahead, though mail is down and in-person voting up almost everywhere.

story.compare_note: Registered-party margin among early ballots, 2026 vs. the same point in 2024, as read from the official files by Call the Map (an independent tracker; Iowa 33,418 ballots through Oct 15, Pennsylvania's 52 comparable counties through Oct 16, Maine 96,849 through Oct 15, Florida's 1,384,887 mail and in-person ballots through Oct 19 against R+4.9 at the same point in 2024). Virginia's early voters are 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (Morris, Oct 12); Ohio's early voters were 41% Democratic and 28% Republican by last primary ballot as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024 (News 5 Cleveland, from Secretary of State data). Florida's, Nevada's, Colorado's, Iowa's, Pennsylvania's and North Carolina's official comparisons with 2022 and 2024 are computed from the state files above. Every state with party registration is more Democratic than at this point in 2024, Florida now included because 2024's Republicans had moved to the mail; against 2022 the picture is mixed and much narrower.

bullets.title: Three states now feed the official comparison with 2022, and together they imply a national vote near even.
bullets.html: By registration, Florida's Oct 20 file counts 1,384,933 ballots at D+4.3 (mail 439,524 Democrats to 372,875 Republicans; in person 139,375 to 146,692), against about D+2.7 at 14 days out in 2022, when in-person voting had not begun; Colorado's 581,822 returned ballots are D+9.0 against D+3.6 on the same day in 2022; Iowa's 15,664 mailed-back absentees are D+34.5 against D+20.4. The app's calibrated slopes turn those into +1.3, +4.5 and +3.1 points of margin and a pooled implied national vote of about D+0.2 (±1.5), against polls at D+8.1. Pennsylvania's mail ballots, 635,088 at D+43.9, meet the 2024 baseline for the first time (D+33.1 at 14 days out), worth about +2.4 (±3.3); its 2022 match comes at 12 days out. Nevada's Oct 20 entry in the UF Election Lab file shows 196,501 ballots split 59,843 Democrats to 59,913 Republicans, an even gap against R+3.6 in 2024, but its mail ballots by party sum to 88,687 of 126,198, fewer Democrats than the day before, so the state's reading and the pooled D+1.2 vs. 2024 should wait for a corrected file.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Oct 20
UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 20)
bullets.aff: Official data; Call the Map is an independent tracker

bullets.title: Nevada: Democrats lead by about 4 points on mail, Republicans win the weekday in-person vote.
bullets.html: Jon Ralston's count had Democrats ahead by 8,354 ballots (5.5 points) of just under 152,000 on the morning of Oct 20, 'a D+5 electorate, which is unheard of' against his R+3 baseline model, after Republicans won the early vote by 13 points on day three in 2022. By the evening the lead was 7,103 of almost 200,000 (about 3.7 points) after Republicans won the day's in-person voting again; two-thirds of ballots are mail, which Democrats win by almost double digits, Clark County's mail by nearly 16. Washoe is D+8 against an R+3 registration; the rurals R+32, at registration. Call the Map reads Clark's mail at D+13.4 through Oct 18 against D+23.2 at the same point in 2022, up 19% in count.
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; county and Secretary of State data

bullets.title: North Carolina's early vote is 38% ahead of 2022, with Republican in-person ballots below four years ago.
bullets.html: Michael Bitzer counts 733,299 accepted ballots through Oct 19, 37.8% above the same day in 2022: in-person voting is up 48% (689,133 vs. 466,681) and mail down 32.6% (44,166 vs. 65,559). Registered Republicans have cast 144,253 in-person ballots against 149,140 at this point in 2022, while Democrats are up 125,877 and unaffiliated voters 100,907; Democrats and unaffiliated voters are 79% of in-person ballots vs. 68% in 2022, and 94 of 100 counties are ahead. G. Elliott Morris puts Democrats at 45.7% of ballots, Republicans at 19.6%, about 18 points more Democratic than the state's usual early-vote norm, with the caution that 2016's 8-point Democratic edge at this stage shrank to 1.8 a week out.
sources: G. Elliott Morris (State Board of Elections file), Oct 20
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan academic and independent data journalist; official data

bullets.title: Georgia passed a million in-person votes, 12% ahead of 2022 at the same point.
bullets.html: The Secretary of State counted 1,007,015 in-person early ballots before noon on Oct 20, up 12% from 894,412 at the same point in 2022, plus 48,916 accepted absentee ballots for 1,055,931 in all (reported by Fox News). The AJC finds Black voters about 35% of the early vote, women ahead of men by about 10 points, about 15% of early voters who skipped 2022, roughly 400,000 from strongly Harris areas vs. 380,000 from strongly Trump ones, and turnout lagging in rural South and Middle Georgia. An RNC spokeswoman says Republicans have cut into Democrats' mail advantage day over day, without figures. Georgia has no party registration.
sources: Fox News live blog (Secretary of State figures), Oct 20
bullets.aff: Official data via a conservative-leaning outlet; AJC is nonpartisan

bullets.title: Texas opened 20% ahead of 2022, with records in the big blue counties.
bullets.html: More than 812,000 Texans voted on the first two days; first-day turnout ran more than 20% above 2022, per Republican data consultant Derek Ryan, who finds 21% of voters with recent Democratic primary histories already voted against 13% with Republican histories, and mail ballots 50% Democratic-history to 30% Republican. Dallas County cast 76,079 first-day ballots vs. 32,605 in 2022 and 59,389 in 2018; Collin 34,500 vs. 18,991; Denton 34,700 vs. 17,416; Travis 4.3% of registered voters vs. 2.8%. Ryan says Republicans need at least 25% of turnout from outside the 25 largest counties. Texas has no party registration.
sources: Fox News live blog (Ryan Data & Research), Oct 20
bullets.aff: Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant; county data via nonpartisan outlets

bullets.title: Florida: Democrats bank the mail, Republicans edge the first in-person days.
bullets.html: The Division of Elections' Oct 20 morning file had 933,867 mail ballots returned, 394,962 from Democrats and 340,591 from Republicans (D+54,371), and 171,015 in-person ballots, 69,280 Republican to 68,650 Democratic; by the evening file in-person voting was 353,809 at R+7,317 and the total gap D+4.3. The in-person lead is small and early, and every county must open sites by Oct 24. Comparisons in the press are to 2022's final mail totals (Democrats 1.19 million of 2.77 million), not the same point.

bullets.title: Turnout without party: Michigan and Wisconsin mail only level with or below 2022, Virginia and Minnesota well ahead.
bullets.html: Michigan had 789,572 ballots back by 7 a.m. Oct 20 (10.7% of active voters) vs. 771,967 at the same time in 2022, up 2.2%, with 2,121,458 requests, 17% ahead; statewide in-person voting opens Oct 24. Wisconsin had 173,164 absentee ballots returned of 364,888 requested on the morning of Oct 19, vs. 195,287 of 438,673 at the same point in 2022; in-person absentee voting began Oct 20. Virginia had more than 568,000 early votes with 21 days to go vs. just over 307,000 at the same stage in 2022 (VPAP), and Minnesota 202,252 accepted ballots through Oct 15 vs. 172,520.
sources: CBS Detroit (Michigan Secretary of State release), Oct 20

bullets.title: The Democratic edge is partly a change in how people vote, and Republicans say they vote later.
bullets.html: Mail is down and in-person voting up almost everywhere: North Carolina's mail ballots are 32.6% below 2022 while in-person is up 48%; Ohio's mail requests trail 2022 by about 240,000 while first-week in-person voting ran nearly four times 2022's; in an NBC poll, 23% of Democrats plan to vote by mail, down from 34% in 2024. In Ohio, GOP county chairman Tony Schroeder says 'we are seeing no evidence that there has been a surge of Democrats anxious to vote,' and a conservative tracker put the Democratic turnout edge there at D+12 after the biggest mail return day; an RNC spokeswoman says Republicans are cutting into Democrats' mail lead in Georgia. Ralston cautions that Nevada Republicans won 2022's Election Day by nearly 50,000 ballots.
bullets.aff: The Daily Signal is a conservative outlet; GOP-aligned claims reported as such

story.calendar_note: Every Florida county must open in-person early voting by Oct 24 (counties could open Oct 19); Michigan's statewide sites, New York's and New Jersey's open Oct 24 and Kentucky's Oct 29. Texas, Alaska, Colorado's service centers and South Carolina opened Oct 19 and Wisconsin's in-person absentee voting Oct 20; Nevada's in-person early voting opened Oct 17, North Carolina's Oct 15 and Georgia's Oct 13. Georgia's and Texas's in-person periods end Oct 30. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire have no early in-person voting.
story.cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 43 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 16-21) when these comparisons were compiled; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
story.signals_verdict: The official same-point comparison with 2022, now Florida, Colorado and Iowa, implies a national vote of about D+0.2 (±1.5): Florida is D+4.3 by registration against about D+2.7 at 14 days out in 2022, Colorado D+9.0 against D+3.6, Iowa's absentee pool D+34.5 against D+20.4; Pennsylvania's first match with 2024 (D+43.9 vs. D+33.1) implies about D+2.4, and Nevada's Oct 20 file reads even against R+3.6 in 2024 but its party counts cover only part of the mail ballots, so that figure and the pooled D+1.2 vs. 2024 are provisional. The early vote fits a Democratic year without confirming polls at D+8.1: Republicans are winning Florida's and Nevada's weekday in-person voting while Democrats bank mail, North Carolina and Georgia run well ahead of 2022 and Texas opened 20% ahead. The next tests are Nevada's corrected file and Clark County's mail, Florida's first full in-person week, Pennsylvania's first 2022 match at 12 days out and Michigan's in-person start on Oct 24.

signals.title: Nevada Democrats lead by about 4 points after four days; Republicans won day three in 2022 by 13
signals.value: Jon Ralston's count on the morning of Oct 20: Democrats ahead by 8,354 ballots, 5.5 points, of just under 152,000 (turnout D 11%, R 9%, others 4%; vote share 40-35-25), with Clark D by nearly 12, Washoe D+8 against R+3 registration and the rurals R+32. By the evening of Oct 20: D+7,103 of almost 200,000, about 3.7 points, after Republicans won the day's in-person vote. He writes that Republicans won the early vote by 13 points on day three in 2022 and led in-person by 9 at this point, 'so this is quite the reversal'; his baseline model was an R+3 electorate and 'if this is true after a few more days, I may have to readjust.'
signals.catch: Party is registration, not vote choice. Two-thirds of ballots are mail, which Democrats win by almost double digits; Republicans have won the weekday in-person vote in every region. Independents run below his model (27%). The state's Oct 20 file in UF Election Lab's compilation reads even, but its mail ballots by party sum to only 88,687 of 126,198, so the app's official Nevada figure is provisional. In 2022 Republicans won Election Day by nearly 50,000 ballots.
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet (Jon Ralston); county and Secretary of State data

signals.title: Georgia's in-person early vote is 12% ahead of 2022 at the same point
signals.value: 1,007,015 in-person early ballots before noon on Oct 20, up 12% from 894,412 at the same point in 2022, per the Secretary of State; with 48,916 accepted absentee ballots, 1,055,931 in all. The AJC: Black voters about 35% of the early vote, women ahead of men by about 10 points, about 15% (160,000) did not vote in 2022, roughly 400,000 from strongly Harris precincts vs. 380,000 from strongly Trump ones (21% of voters there vs. 16%).
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. Mail is a far smaller share than in 2022, which flatters the in-person comparison. The AJC reports turnout lagging in rural South and Middle Georgia and up in Republican-leaning Cherokee and Forsyth. The RNC says Republicans are cutting into Democrats' mail advantage day over day, without figures.
signals.src: Fox News live blog (Secretary of State figures), Oct 20; AJC, Oct 21
signals.aff: Official data via a conservative-leaning outlet; AJC is a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: Ohio's early electorate has flipped from Republican to Democratic
signals.value: Democrats have returned about 94,000 ballots, unaffiliated voters a little more than 67,000 and Republicans nearly 64,000 (by last primary ballot), per the Ohio Capital Journal from Secretary of State data through Oct 12-13; News 5 Cleveland put Democrats at 41% and Republicans at 28% of nearly 230,000 early votes as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024. In-person votes after one week: 194,841 vs. 50,368 in 2022.
signals.catch: 2024 was a presidential year, and Ohio Republicans are shifting from mail to later voting: mail requests are 631,079 vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022. 'Party' is the last primary ballot pulled; seniors are more than half of ballots so far.
signals.src: Ohio Capital Journal (Ohio Secretary of State data), Oct 15; News 5 Cleveland, Oct 13

signals.title: Virginia's early vote is nearly 300,000 ballots ahead of 2022
signals.value: More than 678,000 Virginians had voted by Oct 18, nearly 300,000 more than at the same point in the 2022 midterm (VPAP data via WTVR). Danville has 2,800 vs. a little over 1,000 in 2022.
signals.catch: Virginia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. The count's exact as-of day is not stated. The modeled party lean is in the separate L2 signal.
signals.src: WTVR CBS 6 (Virginia Public Access Project data), Oct 18
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; VPAP is a nonpartisan tracker of state data

signals.title: Maine's absentee vote is 37% ahead of 2022 and slightly more Democratic
signals.value: 126,998 ballots through Oct 19 (67,843 by mail, 68,223 in person): 66,690 Democrats (up 34% on 2022), 25,106 Republicans (up 24%), 35,202 unaffiliated (up 57%). That is a D+32.7 gap vs. D+32.0 at the same working day in 2022; the count is up 37%. Through Oct 15 the gap was D+34.2 vs. D+21.7 at the same point in 2024.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice. The edge over 2022 is less than a point and has narrowed as in-person absentee voting (half the ballots) grows. The 2022 match is by working day.
signals.src: Call the Map (Maine Secretary of State absentee file), Oct 20
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated

signals.title: Minnesota's accepted ballots are running 17% ahead of 2022
signals.value: 202,252 absentee and mail ballots accepted through Oct 15 (80,870 in person, 121,382 by mail), vs. 172,520 at the same point in 2022. 519,813 ballots distributed vs. 474,935.
signals.catch: Minnesota has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. The lead over 2022 has narrowed from 29% (Oct 8). The source is a local news aggregator citing the Secretary of State's Oct 16 report; the report itself was not opened.
signals.src: Minneapolimedia News (Minnesota Secretary of State Oct 16 report), Oct 18
signals.aff: Official data via a local aggregator

signals.title: Pennsylvania's mail vote is less Democratic than at this point in 2022
signals.value: In the 63 counties with comparable files, 632,662 returned mail ballots through Oct 19 are D+44.2 by registration vs. D+53.9 at the same point in 2022: Democrats 423,631 (down 7%), Republicans 147,130 (up 24%), others 55,506 (up 13%), all ballots up 1% (Call the Map, Oct 20). The app's official comparison with 2024 (D+43.9 vs. D+33.1 at 14 days out) runs the other way.
signals.catch: Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year and Democrats are shifting to Election Day voting after the party's own warnings about the mail; the official comparison (above) takes over against 2022 at 12 days out. Older voters dominate the returns so far.
signals.src: Call the Map (Pennsylvania Department of State mail-ballot file), Oct 20
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated

signals.title: Wisconsin's mail returns trail 2022 by 11%, requests by 17%
signals.value: As of the morning of Oct 19, 364,888 absentee ballots had been requested and 173,164 returned, vs. 438,673 requested and 195,287 returned by the same point in 2022 (Wisconsin Elections Commission figures). Earlier, requests were down 29% in Madison and 20% in the city of Milwaukee (WisPolitics, Oct 6).
signals.catch: No party registration. In-person absentee voting started Oct 20 and both parties have pushed voters away from mail, so the gap may close in person. Racine County's returns were down 22% on Oct 18.
signals.src: Wisconsin Examiner (Wisconsin Elections Commission data), Oct 20
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: Michigan's mail returns are 2% ahead of 2022, requests 17% ahead
signals.value: 789,476 ballots returned by mail, drop box or at clerks' offices as of 7 a.m. Oct 20, plus 96 cast at early-voting sites, 789,572 in all (10.7% of active voters), vs. 771,967 at the same time in 2022, up 2.2%; 2,121,458 requests, 2,001,574 from the permanent list, 17% ahead of 2022 (Secretary of State release).
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction. Returns had been 30% ahead of 2022 on Oct 6 and have since converged; statewide in-person early voting opens Oct 24.
signals.src: CBS Detroit (Michigan Secretary of State release), Oct 20
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: Texas opened 20% ahead of 2022; Democratic-primary voters are turning out faster
signals.value: More than 812,000 ballots in the first two days; first-day turnout more than 20% above 2022. About 21% of voters who took part in the last four Democratic primaries had voted, vs. 13% of those with Republican primary histories; of 82,235 mail ballots identified, 50% came from voters with Democratic primary history and 30% Republican (Derek Ryan, Ryan Data & Research). Dallas County 76,079 first-day ballots vs. 32,605 in 2022; Collin 34,500 vs. 18,991; Denton 34,700 vs. 17,416; Travis 4.3% of registered voters vs. 2.8%.
signals.catch: No party registration: primary history covers a minority of voters, and the big counties also hold most Republican suburban voters. Ryan is a Republican consultant; he says Republicans need at least 25% of turnout from outside the 25 largest counties. Day-one surges often fade.
signals.src: Fox News live blog (Ryan Data & Research), Oct 20; KERA, Oct 20; KUT, Oct 20
signals.aff: Derek Ryan is a Republican data consultant; county figures via nonpartisan outlets

signals.title: Florida Republicans edge the first in-person days while Democrats lead the mail
signals.value: Division of Elections file compiled 11:01 a.m. Oct 20: 171,015 in-person ballots, 69,280 Republican, 68,650 Democratic, 28,851 no party, 4,234 other; 933,867 mail ballots returned, 394,962 Democratic, 340,591 Republican (D+54,371), 175,533 no party. By the evening file, in-person voting stood at 353,809 with Republicans ahead by 7,317 and the overall gap at D+4.3.
signals.catch: Only counties that chose to open early are voting; all must by Oct 24. Republicans won Florida's in-person vote by far more in 2022 and 2024, so a near-even start is not obviously good for them; no same-point in-person figure for 2022 was published. Registration is not vote choice. The overall same-point comparison is the app's official panel.
signals.src: CBS Miami, Oct 20; CiberCuba (Division of Elections figures), Oct 20

signals.title: Clark County's mail vote is less Democratic than at this point in 2022
signals.value: Clark County mail ballots through Oct 18: 46,590, Democrats 19,681 (up 3% on 2022), Republicans 13,459 (up 34%), others 13,450 (up 34%), a D+13.4 gap vs. D+23.2 at the same number of days before Election Day in 2022; the count is up 19%. Of 97,990 Clark ballots in the file, 62% were mail and 38% in person (Call the Map). Ralston has Clark's mail at 43-29.
signals.catch: Democrats are shifting from mail to in person, which Ralston's county-wide figures (Clark D by nearly 12 overall) absorb; this compares only the mail mode. Registration is not vote choice. Small numbers for a county of 1.4 million voters.
signals.src: Call the Map (Clark County mail file), Oct 20
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated

sealed.note: SHA-256 fingerprints of the sealed versions of a separate, judgment-based forecast that is kept privately until after Election Day. Hash = SHA-256 of the version's full text (UTF-8) ending with one line break.

watch.note: Maintained daily. Every item links to the page that confirms it.
watch.trail_note: Trump and Vance campaign appearances since Sep 1, 2026, from White House pool reports, Roll Call Factbase and local coverage. Closed-press fundraisers and tele-rallies are rarely reported, so they are undercounted.

happened.title: NYT/Siena: Democrats lead the House ballot 52-41 among likely voters
happened.what: The New York Times/Siena national poll of more than 3,000 voters, released Oct. 21, finds Democrats ahead of Republicans by 10 points on the congressional ballot when every candidate's name is offered (52-41 in the Times' topline, per Fox News and the RealClearPolling table), leading by 5 in the 35 states with Senate races, with Trump's job approval at 36-59.
happened.why: The highest-rated national poll of the cycle lands two points above the polling average, and its Senate-state figure suggests the map's tilt toward Republicans is being overcome.
happened.src: Siena College Research Institute, Oct 21; Fox News live blog, Oct 21

happened.title: Inside Elections shifts 30 races toward Democrats, Texas Senate to Toss-up
happened.what: Inside Elections moved five Senate races (Texas Tilt R to Toss-up, New Hampshire Toss-up to Tilt D, Kansas Likely to Tilt R, South Carolina Likely to Lean R, Florida Solid to Likely R), 22 House races (NC-01, NC-11, OH-09, IA-02 and TX-15 to Toss-up; AZ-01, PA-07 and PA-08 to Tilt D) and three governor races (Texas Likely to Lean R, Nebraska and Vermont Solid to Likely R), projecting a Democratic Senate gain of three to five seats and a House gain of 10 to 20.
happened.why: The rater that had been most favorable to Republicans now puts the four-seat Senate gain Democrats need inside its range and says Democrats have no defensive Senate seat rated Toss-up or worse.

happened.title: Crystal Ball: 223 House seats now at least lean Democratic after 28 changes
happened.what: Sabato's Crystal Ball moved 28 House ratings, pushing seats at least leaning Democratic to 223 against 200 at least leaning Republican and 12 Toss-ups: IA-03, IA-02, WI-03, PA-10, AZ-06, CO-08, AZ-01, NC-01 and NC-11 went from Toss-up to Leans Democratic, TX-35 to Toss-up, and TX-23, NV-02, SC-01 and MN-01 to Leans Republican.
happened.why: For the first time this cycle a major rater has more than 218 seats leaning to Democrats, so Republicans would need to win seats currently rated against them to keep the House.

happened.title: Cook moves South Carolina and Mississippi toward Democrats, Minnesota toward Republicans
happened.what: The Cook Political Report shifted South Carolina from Likely to Lean Republican, Mississippi from Solid to Likely Republican and Minnesota from Likely to Lean Democratic, writing that recent polling shows Peggy Flanagan 'slightly underperforming where she should be given the national environment'; its Senate page now lists seven Toss Ups (Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, Texas), six of them Republican-held.
happened.why: Cook says the moves do not change its overall Senate outlook, but Minnesota becomes the one Democratic-held seat where the rater sees the candidate lagging the environment.

happened.title: DCCC adds three Republican-held districts; Senate Majority PAC buys in Mississippi
happened.what: The DCCC began coordinated television ads in AZ-02, OH-10 and SC-01 as part of a $16 million week, bringing it to 49 districts, about two-thirds held by Republicans; Senate Majority PAC is launching a $1.2 million buy for Scott Colom against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, and the RNC has transferred more than $50 million to the NRCC and NRSC.
happened.why: Democratic committees are spending into districts Trump carried comfortably and a Senate seat no rater had in play a month ago, while Republican money shifts toward defense.
happened.src: Washington Sun (Elena Schneider), Oct 20; Fox News live blog, Oct 20

happened.title: California asks court to reject DOJ bid to hold 20,000 mail ballots
happened.what: Attorney General Rob Bonta filed California's opposition to the Justice Department's request for a restraining order that would segregate up to 20,000 mail ballots from voters a federal list calls likely noncitizens, calling the suit 'a reckless political stunt'; a day earlier federal prosecutors charged 28 green-card holders, 22 of them for voting in past elections. No hearing date has been set.
happened.why: California holds several of the House seats that will decide the majority, and the ruling will test whether federal list-matching can hold ballots after the 90-day limit on systematic roll maintenance.

happened.title: Iowa governor debate postponed after a death in Rob Sand's family
happened.what: The Iowa PBS debate between Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn set for Oct. 21 will not take place after Sand's brother-in-law was killed in a highway crash; Iowa PBS says it may be rescheduled, and a KCRG-TV debate in Cedar Rapids on Oct. 27 remains scheduled. Lahn said 'some things are bigger than politics.'
happened.why: The open Iowa governorship, which Marist had Sand leading 52-45 and co/efficient 49-45, loses one of its two televised debates in the final two weeks.

happened.title: Silver Bulletin moves Senate to Likely Democratic, 75% chance
happened.what: Nate Silver's FLIPR 2026 forecast, published by Silver Bulletin, raised Democrats' chance of winning Senate control to 75%, moving the chamber from Lean D to Likely D.
happened.why: A model that blends polls, fundraising, incumbency and expert ratings now makes Democrats clear favorites to net the four seats they need for a majority.

happened.title: Republicans' ad edge is in Senate races, not the House
happened.what: AdImpact figures analyzed by The New York Times show Republicans outspending Democrats $947 million to $625 million in the seven Senate races Cook rates Toss Ups, including roughly $141 million more in Texas and nearly $90 million more in Ohio, but only about $14 million more across the 21 House Toss Ups, where Democrats lead in 11.
happened.why: The Republican money advantage is concentrated in the Senate, leaving the House battlefield close to even on the air while Democratic candidates outraised Republicans in 38 of the 42 most competitive House races.
happened.src: New York Times via GV Wire, Oct 19

happened.title: Trump promises $5,000 'tariff' checks if Republicans keep Congress
happened.what: At his Dalton, Ga., rally, Trump said every adult citizen would receive $5,000, funded by tariff revenue and to be spent inside the country, if Republicans control both chambers after the midterms; he did not describe a legislative mechanism or timeline.
happened.why: It is the first explicit national promise tied to the outcome of the midterms, made with gasoline above $4 and the economy the top issue in every poll.

happened.title: Cook moves 11 more House races toward Democrats, half in Ohio, Nebraska and Kansas
happened.what: The Cook Political Report moved 11 House ratings, all toward Democrats, saying Republicans' troubles are 'particularly pronounced in Midwestern red states'; its Oct 16 ratings page lists the open MT-01 among 21 Toss Ups (16 Republican-held, 5 Democratic-held), MN-01, OH-10, OH-15, NY-21 and SC-01 as Lean Republican, and KS-02, NE-01 and FL-16 as Likely Republican.
happened.why: The House map keeps widening into Trump districts in states that also host competitive Senate races, so Republican money is being pulled in two directions.

happened.title: Musk is the donor behind SLF's $200 million Texas rescue
happened.what: Elon Musk gave Senate Leadership Fund $75 million on Sept. 9 and about $83 million two weeks later, money SLF routed into a 'Texas PAC' that has spent more than $159 million on ads for Ken Paxton and plans nearly $200 million, on top of $18.8 million from Musk's America PAC, mostly against James Talarico.
happened.why: Republicans are spending at a presidential scale to hold a Senate seat Trump carried by 14 points, money that is not going to Maine, Iowa, Ohio or Kansas.

upcoming.title: Rogers, El-Sayed hold second Michigan Senate debate
upcoming.what: WXYZ-TV hosts the second debate between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed at 7 p.m. from its Broadcast House studios in Detroit, airing statewide and streaming on WXYZ Channel 7 and WXMI Fox 17.
upcoming.why: It comes three days before statewide early voting begins in Michigan.

upcoming.title: Vermont Public hosts governor debate
upcoming.what: Vermont Public's gubernatorial debate airs live at 7 p.m. from its Winooski studios, hosted by Mikaela Lefrak, on its radio and television channels, streams and YouTube, with rebroadcasts Oct. 22.
upcoming.why: Cook moved the Vermont governor race from Solid to Likely Republican on Oct. 13, one of the Republican-held governorships Democrats would need for a majority.

upcoming.title: Marshall, Hamilton debate on Kansas Nexstar stations
upcoming.what: Sen. Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton debate from 7 to 8 p.m. Central, originating at WDAF-TV in Kansas City and airing on Nexstar stations in Kansas City, Topeka, Wichita and Joplin; Libertarian David Graham is not included.
upcoming.why: Cook rates the race a Toss Up, and both parties' main Senate super PACs are now spending on it.
upcoming.src: FOX4 Kansas City, Sep 29; Kansas Reflector, Oct 19

upcoming.title: Crowley, Tiffany hold Wisconsin governor debate
upcoming.what: WISN-12 hosts a one-hour debate between Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany at Marquette University at 7 p.m. local time, also carried by partner stations in Green Bay, Madison, Wausau, Eau Claire and La Crosse.
upcoming.why: Tiffany has said one debate is sufficient, making this likely the only televised matchup in the open governor race.

upcoming.title: Klobuchar, Demuth debate for Minnesota governor
upcoming.what: Amy Klobuchar and Lisa Demuth meet for a 60-minute debate at 7 p.m. Central, live from KTTC/KXLT in Rochester, co-produced by FOX 9 and Gray Media stations and streamed on FOX9.com, the FOX LOCAL app and FOX 9's YouTube channel.
upcoming.why: It is the first scheduled debate in the open governor race, where Klobuchar led Demuth 50-41 in the Mason-Dixon poll ending Oct. 7.

upcoming.title: FEC pre-general reports due
upcoming.what: Pre-general reports covering Oct. 1 through Oct. 14 are due to the FEC.
upcoming.why: They provide the last full look at campaign and committee cash and spending before Election Day.

upcoming.title: Alvarado, Dembo debate in Kentucky's 6th District
upcoming.what: Republican Alvarado and Democrat Dembo, the KY-06 nominees, debate on WDKY (FOX 56) at 7 p.m.
upcoming.why: Inside Elections rates the open KY-06 Lean Republican, one of the Republican-held seats on the edge of the House battlefield.

upcoming.title: Maine Public interviews Dunlap in ME-02 after LePage declines debate
upcoming.what: Maine Public airs a 30-minute live interview with Democrat Matt Dunlap at 7 p.m. in place of a ME-02 debate, which Republican Paul LePage declined.
upcoming.why: The open ME-02, which Inside Elections moved to Lean Republican on Oct. 20, is one of the Republican targets Democrats need to hold or flip for a larger majority.

upcoming.title: Arizona mail-ballot request deadline
upcoming.what: Oct. 23 is the last day to request a mail ballot in Arizona; Oct. 27 is the last recommended day to mail it back, and in-person early voting ends Oct. 30.
upcoming.why: Arizona's governor race, rated Lean Democrat by Cook, and the AZ-01 and AZ-06 House seats are on the competitive list.

upcoming.title: University of Michigan final October consumer sentiment
upcoming.what: The University of Michigan releases its final October consumer-sentiment reading; the preliminary figure was 46.3, near the survey's record low.
upcoming.why: It is the last sentiment reading before Election Day in a campaign dominated by prices, with gasoline above $4.

upcoming.title: Michigan statewide early voting begins
upcoming.what: Early in-person voting sites open statewide in Michigan, open at least eight hours a day through Nov. 1, with some communities offering extra days.
upcoming.why: Early votes start in the open Senate and governor races and in House battlegrounds such as MI-04 and MI-07.

upcoming.title: Florida mandatory early voting begins
upcoming.what: Florida's mandatory early voting period runs Oct. 24 through Oct. 31, and counties may offer additional days or hours.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in the Senate race, a governor race Cook moved to Lean Republican, and House seats such as FL-13 and FL-27.

upcoming.title: Obama rallies in Cleveland and Detroit
upcoming.what: Former President Barack Obama is to campaign in Cleveland with Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton and in Detroit with Abdul El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson on Oct. 24, the first Saturday of Michigan's statewide early voting; venues and times are to be announced.
upcoming.why: Ohio's Senate and governor races and Michigan's Senate race are Cook Toss Ups, and Trump and Vance have each campaigned in both states in October.

upcoming.title: New York and New Jersey early voting begins
upcoming.what: Early in-person voting runs Oct. 24 through Nov. 1 in both states; Oct. 24 is also New York's deadline for registration and for mailed or online early mail-ballot applications.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in House battlegrounds including NY-17, a Cook Toss Up, and NJ-07, where the main House GOP super PAC cut its ads.
upcoming.src: New Jersey Division of Elections, accessed Oct 19; Stony Brook University, accessed Oct 19

upcoming.title: Pennsylvania mail ballot application deadline
upcoming.what: Oct. 27 is the deadline to apply for a mail-in or absentee ballot in Pennsylvania, and completed ballots must reach county election offices by 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.
upcoming.why: Pennsylvania's House battlegrounds, including PA-01, PA-07 and PA-08, could help decide House control.
upcoming.src: Pennsylvania Department of State, accessed Oct 13

upcoming.title: Ohio absentee application deadline
upcoming.what: Absentee ballot applications must reach county boards by 8:30 p.m. on Oct. 27; early in-person voting runs extended hours Oct. 26-30, and mail ballots must arrive by 7:30 p.m. on Nov. 3.
upcoming.why: Ohio's Senate race between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown and its open governor race are both Cook Toss Ups.
upcoming.src: Ohio Secretary of State, accessed Oct 14

upcoming.title: Sand, Lahn debate on KCRG in Cedar Rapids
upcoming.what: Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn meet in a KCRG-TV debate in Cedar Rapids, now the first scheduled debate in the race after the Oct. 21 Iowa PBS debate was postponed.
upcoming.why: Iowa's open governorship is one of the competitive governor races, with Sand leading in the Marist and co/efficient polls.

upcoming.title: Nunn, Trone Garriott debate in Iowa's 3rd District
upcoming.what: Rep. Zach Nunn and Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott debate on KCCI at 9 p.m. Central.
upcoming.why: It is the only scheduled debate in a Republican-held Des Moines seat the DCCC has targeted with coordinated ads.

upcoming.title: Obama rallies in Atlanta for Ossoff, Bottoms
upcoming.what: Former President Barack Obama headlines a rally in Atlanta for Sen. Jon Ossoff and governor nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms; the location is to be emailed to RSVPs 24 hours ahead.
upcoming.why: It comes in the last days of Georgia's early voting, with a Toss Up governor race on the ballot and Senate super PACs on both sides off Georgia broadcast TV.

upcoming.title: Maine no-excuse absentee voting period ends
upcoming.what: Oct. 29 is the last day of Maine's no-excuse absentee period, including in-person absentee voting at town and city halls.
upcoming.why: The deadline shapes early ballots in the Collins-Jackson Senate race and the ME-02 House race.

upcoming.title: Kentucky early in-person voting begins
upcoming.what: Kentucky's three days of no-excuse early in-person voting run Thursday, Oct. 29, through Saturday, Oct. 31.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in the open KY-06, which Inside Elections moved to Tilt Republican on Oct. 20, and the Barr-Booker Senate race.

upcoming.title: Pingree, Russell debate in Maine's 1st District
upcoming.what: Maine Public hosts a debate between Rep. Chellie Pingree and Republican Ron Russell at 7 p.m. on its radio, television and streams.
upcoming.why: It is the only scheduled debate in a Democratic-held seat that becomes competitive only in a Republican year.

upcoming.title: Bresnahan debates Democratic challenger on WVIA in PA-08
upcoming.what: WVIA hosts a PA-08 debate in Pittston at 7 p.m. between Rep. Rob Bresnahan and his Democratic challenger.
upcoming.why: Cook rates PA-08 a Toss Up and Inside Elections moved it to Tilt Democratic on Oct. 20; it is one of the Republican-held seats Democrats need for a majority.

upcoming.title: Georgia and Texas in-person early voting ends
upcoming.what: Friday, Oct. 30, is the last day of in-person early voting in Georgia and in Texas.
upcoming.why: The final early-vote totals in two Senate battlegrounds and the Georgia and Texas governor races set the Election Day math for both parties.
upcoming.src: Axios Atlanta, Oct 19; FOX 7 Austin, Oct 12

upcoming.title: Nevada polls close; Alaska follows after midnight ET
upcoming.what: Polls close at 10 p.m. ET in Nevada and Montana; most of Alaska closes at midnight ET and the Aleutian Islands at 1 a.m. ET on Nov. 4.
upcoming.why: Alaska's Senate race, rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections, is likely to be among the last competitive contests to report.

upcoming.title: First polls close in Indiana and Kentucky
upcoming.what: Polls in the Eastern time portions of Indiana and Kentucky close at 6 p.m. ET, with the rest of both states closing at 7 p.m. ET.
upcoming.why: The first returns of the night include House races such as KY-06, which Inside Elections moved to Lean Republican.

upcoming.title: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Virginia, most of Florida
upcoming.what: Polls close at 7 p.m. ET in Georgia, South Carolina, Virginia and Vermont, in most of Florida (the western Panhandle at 8 p.m. ET) and at most New Hampshire polling places (all by 8 p.m. ET).
upcoming.why: First returns arrive in the Georgia, South Carolina, Florida and New Hampshire Senate races and the Georgia and Florida governor races.

upcoming.title: Polls close in North Carolina and Ohio
upcoming.what: Polls close at 7:30 p.m. ET in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia.
upcoming.why: Results begin in the North Carolina and Ohio Senate races and the Ohio governor race.

upcoming.title: Polls close in Maine, Pennsylvania, most of Michigan, Texas
upcoming.what: Polls close at 8 p.m. ET in Maine, Pennsylvania and the rest of New Hampshire, and in most of Michigan, Texas and Kansas, whose westernmost areas close at 9 p.m. ET.
upcoming.why: First results arrive in the Maine, Michigan, Texas and Kansas Senate races and the Michigan and Texas governor races.

upcoming.title: Polls close in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, Wisconsin, Arizona
upcoming.what: Polls close at 9 p.m. ET in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, Wisconsin and Arizona.
upcoming.why: Results begin in the Iowa, Minnesota and Nebraska Senate races and the Iowa, Wisconsin and Arizona governor races.

comps.note: The generic ballot is D+8.8. Three weeks out it has overstated Democrats by 2.6 points on average (weighted to midterms and recent years); it ran too Democratic in 11 of 14 elections since 1998.

comps.label: Approval and the midterm swing
comps.note: Midterms since 1950: the president's party loses ground, more when the president is unpopular. Trump's net approval is −22.

comps.label: Special elections
comps.note: Democrats have beaten the 2024 presidential margin by 12.5 points in this cycle's special elections. In 2006, 2018 and 2022 specials overstated the eventual swing by 3.9 points on average, so that much is taken off.

comps.label: 2025 Virginia and New Jersey governors
comps.note: Both states moved 9.0 points toward Democrats from 2024. The off-year governor races have pointed the right way before every midterm since 2006, with large misses in size.

items.label: Consumer sentiment (University of Michigan)
items.say: Near the lowest readings in the survey's history; sentiment has been low under both parties since 2022.

items.label: Gasoline, national average (AAA)
items.compare: $3.048 a year ago; $4.333 a week ago; $4.479 a month ago
items.say: Up about 40% in a year, though about 7 cents lower than a week ago and 21 cents below a month ago.

items.label: A Chipotle chicken burrito bowl
items.say: Roughly 15–20% more than four years ago; restaurant prices overall are up 3.4% in the past year (CPI food away from home, August).
items.src: Reuters via ThePricer (May 2026); Food Business News (Oct 2022)

items.label: Prediction markets: Democratic House
items.compare: Senate: about 65% Democratic from the balance-of-power contracts (Democrats win both 64.5¢ on Kalshi and Polymarket; Democratic House with Republican Senate 26.5¢ and 27.5¢; Republican House with Democratic Senate under 1¢; Republicans win both 9.2¢ and 8.5¢)
items.say: Markets sit between the polls-only model and the expert raters.

items.label: Cook Political Report House ratings
items.compare: Cook's likely range (Oct 9): Democrats gain 9-19 seats, 224-234; after 11 more moves toward Democrats on Oct 16: Solid/Likely/Lean D 214, Toss Up 21, Lean/Likely/Solid R 200. Senate (Oct 20): 7 Toss Ups, 6 Republican-held, after South Carolina and Mississippi moved toward Democrats and Minnesota toward Republicans
items.say: Democrats need a fifth of the toss-ups for a majority if the seats leaning their way hold.

items.label: House members not seeking re-election
items.say: More Republicans leaving, including 20 running for other office; retirements have not tracked the swing in past midterms.
